events: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji
title: Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji: the last days at Kartarpur
desc: How Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji spent his last years farming at Kartarpur, passed the Guruship to Guru Angad Dev Ji and merged with the Divine Light in 1539, and the day.
kw: Guru Nanak Dev Ji Joti Jot
alt: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Kartarpur, in Narowal district of Pakistan
cap: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Kartarpur, where Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji spent his last years
body: The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji remembers the day in 1539 when the founder of the Sikh faith completed his life on earth at Kartarpur, on the right bank of the Ravi, and merged with the Divine Light. Sikhs speak of the passing of a Guru as joti jot, light merging into light.
## Kartarpur, the town of the Creator

After more than twenty years of travelling on his udasis, Guru Nanak Dev Ji settled at Kartarpur, a town he founded, and spent about eighteen years there. He took off the dress of a traveller and worked the fields himself, showing that a spiritual life is lived in the middle of ordinary work and family. The day began before dawn with Japji Sahib and kirtan, and closed with Sodar and Arti; in between, everyone who came ate together in the langar. Here Bhai Lehna Ji served him and was chosen as Guru Angad.
## The sheet of flowers

Sikh tradition remembers that as the Guru's end drew near, his Hindu followers wished to cremate him and his Muslim followers to bury him. The Guru asked each group to place flowers on either side of him, and said that those whose flowers were still fresh in the morning could perform the rites. In the morning both sets of flowers were fresh, and when the sheet was lifted the body was gone. The sheet was divided, and today a samadh and a grave stand side by side at Kartarpur.
## How the day is observed

Sangats remember the day with kirtan, katha and Ardas in Punjab and around the world. Since the Kartarpur Corridor opened in 2019, pilgrims from India can visit Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, Kartarpur, without a visa, and many make the journey on or near this day.

events: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji (fixed solar anniversary)
title: Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji: thirteen years at Khadur Sahib
desc: Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji completed his life at Khadur Sahib in 1552 after passing the Guruship to Sri Guru Amar Das Ji. His work for Gurmukhi and langar, and the day.
kw: Guru Angad Dev Ji Joti Jot
alt: A Sikh congregation gathered around Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, about 1900
cap: A Sikh congregation at a katha in Tarn Taran district, around 1900
body: The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji remembers the day in 1552 when the second Sikh Guru completed his life on earth at Khadur Sahib, near the river Beas, having entrusted the Guruship to Sri Guru Amar Das Ji. The SGPC's Nanakshahi calendar keeps the anniversary on a fixed solar date.
## What he left the Sikhs

In about thirteen years as Guru, Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji gave the young community much of its early shape. He developed and spread the Gurmukhi script, so that the bani could be written and read by ordinary people, and opened schools where children learned to read it. He gathered the hymns of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, and tradition credits him with collecting the accounts of the first Guru's life that grew into the Janamsakhis. He encouraged wrestling and physical fitness, and kept an akhara at Khadur Sahib for the young men of the village.

Mata Khivi Ji, his wife, ran the langar at Khadur Sahib, where everyone who came was fed, and she is the only woman named in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, in a Vaar by Bhai Satta and Bhai Balvand that praises the rich kheer of her kitchen. Under her care the langar became a daily feature of Sikh life.
## Choosing his successor
Like Guru Nanak Dev Ji before him, Guru Angad Dev Ji passed over his own sons, Dasu and Datu, and chose the elderly Amar Das Ji, who had served him for twelve years.
## How the day is observed
Sangats gather for kirtan and Ardas at Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Khadur Sahib, and in gurdwaras everywhere, to remember his life of service.

events: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Amar Das Ji / Goindwal Sahib Jorh Mela
title: Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji and the Goindwal Sahib Jorh Mela
desc: Sri Guru Amar Das Ji completed his life at Goindwal Sahib in 1574, aged ninety-five. His work, the baoli of eighty-four steps, and the Jorh Mela held there on the day.
kw: Guru Amar Das Ji Joti Jot
alt: Gurdwara Baoli Sahib at Goindwal Sahib
cap: Gurdwara Baoli Sahib, Goindwal, built by Sri Guru Amar Das Ji
body: The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Amar Das Ji remembers the day in 1574 when the third Sikh Guru completed his life on earth at Goindwal Sahib, at the age of about ninety-five, having entrusted the Guruship to Sri Guru Ram Das Ji. The day is marked by a Jorh Mela at Goindwal Sahib.
## Twenty-two years as Guru

Sri Guru Amar Das Ji became Guru in his seventies and led the Sikhs for about twenty-two years. He made Goindwal Sahib the centre of the faith and built its baoli, a step-well reached by eighty-four steps. He made langar a condition of meeting him, so that rich and poor, high caste and low, sat in one line and ate the same food. He divided the growing community into twenty-two manjis, appointed preachers among them women, spoke against sati and purdah, and set Vaisakhi, Diwali and Maghi as days when Sikhs gathered at Goindwal. He composed Anand Sahib, sung at the close of every Sikh service and at every Anand Karaj.
## The passing of the Guruship

Before his passing he chose his son-in-law, Bhai Jetha Ji, over his own sons, and asked the family and the sangat to bow to him as Guru Ram Das. Tradition remembers that he asked that no one weep for him, but that kirtan be sung instead.
## The Jorh Mela at Goindwal

Pilgrims come to Goindwal Sahib in large numbers for the Jorh Mela. Many walk down the eighty-four steps of the baoli and recite Japji Sahib once on each step, a practice tradition links to freedom from the cycle of eighty-four lakh births, and bathe in its water. Gurdwaras everywhere hold kirtan and Ardas.

events: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Ram Das Sahib Ji
title: Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji: the founder of Amritsar
desc: Sri Guru Ram Das Ji completed his life at Goindwal Sahib in 1581 after naming Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji as Guru. The city he founded, the Laavan, and the day.
kw: Guru Ram Das Ji Joti Jot
alt: Gurdwara Baoli Sahib at Goindwal in an early photograph
body: The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Ram Das Ji remembers the day in 1581 when the fourth Sikh Guru completed his life on earth at Goindwal Sahib, after entrusting the Guruship to his youngest son, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji. He was forty-seven, and had been Guru for about seven years.
## A city and a sarovar

In those seven years Sri Guru Ram Das Ji founded the town first called Guru Ka Chakk and then Ramdaspur, which grew into Amritsar. He had the sarovar dug, the pool of nectar that gave the city its name, around which his son would raise Sri Harmandir Sahib. He invited traders and craftsmen of fifty-two trades to settle there, and the bazaar he founded, Guru Bazaar, still stands. He appointed masands to look after distant sangats and collect their offerings for the Guru's work.
## His bani

His bani in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is sung in thirty raags and is known for its tenderness and longing. It includes the Laavan, the four hymns around which the couple walk at an Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding, and a number of the shabads Sikhs recite in Rehras Sahib and Sohila Sahib each evening.
## Choosing Guru Arjan Dev Ji

His eldest son, Prithi Chand, wanted the Guruship and resented the choice; his second son, Mahadev, had turned to an ascetic life. The Guru chose Arjan Dev Ji, whose letters of longing from Lahore had shown his devotion, and asked Baba Budha Ji to perform the ceremony before the sangat.
## How the day is observed
Sangats remember him with kirtan, katha and Ardas at Goindwal Sahib, at Amritsar and in gurdwaras everywhere.

events: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji (fixed solar anniversary)
title: Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji: the last years at Kiratpur Sahib
desc: Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji completed his life at Kiratpur Sahib in 1644 after the longest Guruship of the ten Gurus. Patalpuri Sahib, his legacy, and the day.
kw: Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji Joti Jot
alt: Gurdwara Patalpuri Sahib on the banks of the Sutlej at Kiratpur
cap: Gurdwara Patalpuri Sahib, Kiratpur, where the last rites of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji took place
body: The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji remembers the day in 1644 when the sixth Sikh Guru completed his life on earth at Kiratpur Sahib, on the banks of the Sutlej. His Guruship of about thirty-eight years was the longest of the ten Gurus. The SGPC's Nanakshahi calendar keeps the anniversary on a fixed solar date.
## A Guruship of Miri and Piri

Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji became Guru as a boy after the shaheedi of his father, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, and changed the course of Sikh history. He wore two swords for Miri and Piri, built Sri Akal Takht Sahib, raised a body of armed Sikhs and fought four battles of defence against Mughal forces. Imprisoned at Gwalior, he secured the release of fifty-two kings along with his own, which Sikhs remember at Bandi Chhor Divas. He also travelled to preach, as far as Kashmir and Pilibhit.
## Kiratpur Sahib

In his last decade he settled at Kiratpur Sahib, a town founded on land given by the Raja of Kahlur, and lived there in relative peace. His eldest son, Baba Gurditta Ji, passed away before him, and the Guru chose Baba Gurditta's younger son, Har Rai Ji, as his successor, recognising his gentleness and devotion. Before his passing he asked his followers to accept the boy as Guru.
## How the day is observed

Gurdwara Patalpuri Sahib at Kiratpur, where his last rites took place on the bank of the Sutlej, is visited by many on the day; it is also where many Sikh families bring the ashes of their loved ones. Sangats hold kirtan and Ardas there and in gurdwaras everywhere.

events: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji
title: Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji: the gentle Guru of Kiratpur
desc: Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji completed his life at Kiratpur Sahib in 1661 after naming his young son Harkrishan Ji as Guru. His love of nature, his healing and the day.
kw: Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji Joti Jot
alt: Gurdwara Charan Kamal at Kiratpur Sahib
body: The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji remembers the day in 1661 when the seventh Sikh Guru completed his life on earth at Kiratpur Sahib, aged about thirty-one, after entrusting the Guruship to his younger son, Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji.
## The gentlest of the Gurus

Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji was the grandson of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji and is remembered for his tenderness towards every living thing. He kept gardens and a small zoo at Kiratpur Sahib, and a dispensary of herbal medicines open to anyone in need. Sikh tradition tells that when Dara Shikoh, the eldest son of the emperor Shah Jahan, fell gravely ill and the court physicians could do nothing, the Guru sent the herbs that healed him, saying that a tree gives shade even to the one who cuts it.
## A Guruship of preaching

He kept a body of about two thousand mounted Sikhs, as his grandfather had wished, but his years as Guru were largely peaceful. He travelled through the Malwa and the Doaba, and sent preachers further afield; among those he blessed was Phul, from whom the ruling families of Patiala, Nabha and Jind later descended.
## The succession

Summoned to the court of the emperor Aurangzeb, the Guru sent his elder son Ram Rai instead. When Ram Rai altered a line of the Guru's bani to please the court, the Guru disowned him and chose his younger son, Harkrishan Ji, then five, as the eighth Guru.
## How the day is observed
Sikhs remember him with kirtan and Ardas at Kiratpur Sahib and in gurdwaras everywhere, and katha often turns to his compassion and his care for nature.

events: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji
title: Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji: serving the sick in Delhi
desc: The eighth Guru served the sick of Delhi through an epidemic and passed away in 1664, aged about eight, after naming Baba Bakale. Bangla Sahib, Bala Sahib and the day.
kw: Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji Joti Jot
alt: Front view of Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi
cap: Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, Delhi, the bungalow where Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji stayed
body: The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji remembers the day in 1664 when the eighth Sikh Guru, still a child of about eight, completed his life on earth in Delhi. Sikhs remember him as the Bal Guru, and for the compassion he showed the sick in his last days.
## Called to Delhi

His elder brother, Ram Rai, disputed his Guruship and asked the emperor Aurangzeb to intervene, and the young Guru was summoned to Delhi. Raja Jai Singh of Amber, a noble at the court, offered him his bungalow in the city, where Gurdwara Bangla Sahib now stands. Tradition remembers that the Guru never met the emperor, and that the Raja's queen, testing him, dressed as a maid among her attendants, and the child walked past the others to sit in her lap.
## Serving the sick

That year smallpox and cholera spread through Delhi. The Guru went among the sick of every faith, comforting them and giving them water from the well at the bungalow, and many recovered. He caught smallpox himself. As he lay ill, the sangat asked who would lead them after him. He asked for five paise and a coconut, moved them in a circle, and said only Baba Bakale, the Baba is at Bakala, pointing to his great-uncle, Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji.
## How the day is observed

His last rites took place on the bank of the Yamuna, where Gurdwara Bala Sahib now stands. Sangats gather for kirtan, katha and Ardas at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib and Gurdwara Bala Sahib, many praying for those who are ill, and take home water from the sarovar at Bangla Sahib.

events: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Gobind Singh Sahib Ji
title: Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji: the last days at Nanded
desc: Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji completed his life at Nanded in 1708 after passing the Guruship to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and the Khalsa. His last year and the day.
kw: Guru Gobind Singh Ji Joti Jot
alt: Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib at Nanded, Maharashtra
cap: Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib, Nanded, where Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji completed his life
body: The Joti Jot Purab of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji remembers the day in October 1708 when the tenth Sikh Guru completed his life on earth at Nanded, on the banks of the Godavari in the Deccan, some weeks after he was wounded by an assassin. Before his passing he gave the Guruship to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and the Guru Khalsa Panth.
## The road to Nanded

In the years before, the Guru had lost his father, his mother and all four of his sons, and had left Anandpur Sahib. After the death of the emperor Aurangzeb in 1707, his successor Bahadur Shah invited the Guru to meet him, and the Guru travelled south with the emperor's camp. At Nanded he met an ascetic, Madho Das Bairagi, who became his Sikh, took the name Banda Singh, and was sent to Punjab to lead the Khalsa.
## The last days

Two Pathans, believed to have been sent by Wazir Khan of Sirhind, came to the Guru's camp, and one stabbed him. The wound was stitched and began to heal, but it opened again when the Guru drew a heavy bow. Knowing his time had come, he gathered the sangat, placed five paise and a coconut before Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, bowed to it, and told the Sikhs that the Granth was now their Guru and the Khalsa its body. Tradition remembers his last instructions as asking the Sikhs to sing kirtan rather than mourn.
## How the day is observed

Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib, one of the five Takhts, stands at the place. Sangats gather there and in gurdwaras around the world for kirtan, katha and Ardas, remembering a life given wholly to the Panth.

events: Akāl Chāṇā / Merging of Bhai Mardana Ji
title: Bhai Mardana Ji: the rababi who walked with Guru Nanak Dev Ji
desc: The life of Bhai Mardana Ji, the Muslim minstrel who played the rabab for Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji on every udasi, and how Sikhs remember his passing.
body: This day remembers the passing of Bhai Mardana Ji, the companion of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji for most of his life and the first musician of the Sikh tradition. Sikhs speak of his akal chalana, his departure into the timeless, and of his merging with the Divine.
## The minstrel of Talwandi

Bhai Mardana Ji was born in 1459 at Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib, into a family of Muslim mirasis, hereditary musicians. He was about ten years older than Guru Nanak Dev Ji and knew him from childhood. When the Guru set out on his long journeys, the udasis, Bhai Mardana Ji went with him, carrying the rabab, a stringed instrument. The Guru sang the bani as it came to him, and Bhai Mardana Ji set it to music; the Janamsakhis tell that the Guru would say, Mardana, play the rabab, the bani is coming.
## Companion on every road

For more than two decades the two travelled together, east to Assam, south to Sri Lanka, north into the mountains and west to Mecca and Baghdad. The Janamsakhis tell many stories of their journeys, of hunger and danger shared, and of the Guru's affection for his friend. In the Vaar in Raag Bihagara of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, three shaloks of Guru Nanak Dev Ji are headed with his companion's name, Mardana. Accounts differ on where he died: some name Kartarpur, others the banks of the Kurram in Afghanistan during the journeys. Tradition holds that the Guru performed his last rites himself.
## How he is remembered

His descendants, the rababis, kept singing kirtan at Sikh shrines for centuries. Sikhs remember his devotion with kirtan, often with the rabab and other string instruments in the old style, and with Ardas in gurdwaras.
